activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: In bear country, parks such as Yosemite count anything with a scent as 'food', so toothpaste, sunscreen and trash must go in the bear locker too.
story:
Lily knelt beside the tent at their campsite in the national park, stuffing her toothbrush into her bag, when she noticed something odd. Their bear locker, the big steel box a few steps away, stood open, and her father was carrying armfuls of stuff toward it. Not just food. He put in the sunscreen, the trash bag, even her little sister's cherry lip balm.

"Why the lip balm?" Lily asked. "That's not food."

Dad set it on the locker shelf. "Here they count anything with a scent as food. Toothpaste, sunscreen, trash, all of it goes in the bear locker too."

Lily thought about that all through dinner. A bear couldn't know what toothpaste was. It just followed smells. That meant her minty toothpaste, left in the tent, would be like a signpost pointing straight at her sleeping bag. She remembered her friend Jazmin saying her family's trip had been ruined by a raccoon, just a raccoon, and this park had actual bears. Bears she would never see coming in the dark.

So she tested her idea. She carried every scented thing she could find to the locker: soap, hand sanitizer, the wrapper from her granola bar, even her strawberry shampoo. Her classmate Davin, camping two sites over with his uncle, wandered past and watched her line the items up. "That's a lot of stuff for somebody who hasn't eaten dinner yet," he said.

"It's not food," Lily said. "It's everything a nose could find." Davin looked at the row of bottles, then at his own tent, and jogged back to check his family's supplies. He returned holding a tube of toothpaste and gave her a thumbs up.

That night Lily lay in her sleeping bag feeling optimistic. The tent smelled like nothing but canvas and dust. In the morning, the ranger stopped by to say a bear had visited the campground, and Lily noticed only one tent had a torn screen, the one far down the row. She watched a gray jay land on the locker's steel top, peck twice at nothing, and fly off into the pines.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A reverse image search can show where a photo appeared online before, which can reveal that an old picture is being passed off as new.
story:
Ella slid her phone under the table for the third time, and her mother gave her the look that meant put it away. "It's important," Ella said. "Everyone's sharing this flood picture from the storm downtown. The whole riverfront is underwater. Zakariya's mom works there, and he can't reach her." Her father set down his fork. "Then put the phone on the table where we can all see it," he said, "and eat while you look."

The photo was dramatic and distinct: brown water swallowing the steps of the library, a stop sign showing only its tip. Her little brother leaned over her arm, wanting to feel part of it, so she angled the screen toward him. Last summer, Ella remembered, a kid at camp had shown them a shark photo that was supposedly from that morning's news; by afternoon the whole cabin had learned the shark had been swimming through the same street in pictures from years before. Someone had typed the address of a search page into the old camp laptop and dragged the photo in. "A reverse image search," the kid had called it. Ella had thought it was a neat trick then. Now she opened the same kind of page, dropped the flood picture in, and waited, chewing bread her brother had quietly pushed onto her plate because she'd forgotten to take any.

The results stacked up. The library flood photo had appeared online years before, back when her brother was small, under a headline about an older storm. It wasn't from today at all. "It's an old picture being passed off as new," she said. "Zakariya's worrying over nothing that happened this week." Her father rubbed his knee, the one where the cartilage had worn thin, and stood up. "Then call him. Tell his family before they panic over an old photo."

Zakariya answered on the first ring. "My mom's fine," he said, before Ella could even speak. "She texted two minutes ago. She's dry. But thank you, thank you for checking." Ella set the phone face up on the table and finally took a real bite of dinner. Her brother mimicked her, cutting his chicken with exaggerated care, and slid the last piece of bread onto her plate.

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: A five-paragraph essay has an introduction, three body paragraphs and a conclusion.
story:
Isabella slid her draft across the library table just as Mr. Tran called out, "Ten minutes until we read our essays aloud, everyone!"

The topic was whether the school should keep its bike racks, and Isabella had written with all her heart. There was the story of her cousin who biked to school in the rain, a paragraph about pollution, a paragraph about how bikes give kids freedom, a paragraph about her neighbor who sold her old bike at a yard sale, and a page of other things she couldn't bear to cut. She counted her paragraphs and her stomach dropped. Seven. Somehow she had seven.

Across the table, Maram was calmly stapling her paper. "How many do you have?" Isabella asked, hoping for company in her misery.

"Five," Maram said. "My sister told me the trick. A five-paragraph essay has an introduction, three body paragraphs and a conclusion." She held up her fingers one at a time. "One, three, one. If you're over or under, something needs to move."

Isabella looked at her pages. She couldn't see why five worked and seven didn't; there was no rule posted anywhere, no diagram in her notebook. But maybe it was like a recipe. If a cake called for three eggs, you didn't add five just because you liked eggs. She had to test it. She labeled her first paragraph "introduction," her last "conclusion," and circled the middle five. Then she tried squeezing her neighbor's bike story into the freedom paragraph, the way Lindsey had once delegated half her poster drawings to Maram when the deadline got close.

"Ms. Popularity over here has five paragraphs," Lindsey announced, pointing at Maram, whose reputation in writing club was so solid that even her stapled essays looked confident.

"That's because I follow the recipe," Maram said. "Unlike Isabella, who is writing a spontaneous novel."

"One, three, one," Isabella muttered, cutting and taping. The rain story went. The yard sale went. At last she counted again: five.

When Mr. Tran called her name, Isabella stood up, took a breath, and read her first line aloud: "Every kid at this school deserves a safe place to park a bike."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Pigs have very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water to cool off on hot days.
story:
The bus let them off in front of the science center, where a banner read Living Farms Week. Sadie's class had studied electricity all month, so Mr. Popescu surprised them by leading the line straight past the lightning dome and toward a hot, glassy hall that smelled of straw. In a low pen, two pink pigs lay belly-down in a wide puddle of mud, blinking at the crowd.

"They're filthy," said Nadine, wrinkling her nose. "Why would anybody show off dirty pigs?"

Sadie leaned on the rail. The hall was warm from the sun through the glass roof, and the pigs' mud was dark and wet. On the wall, a screen showed a big view of pigskin, and a small sign sat below it. She read it twice. Then she noticed something: the pigs had flopped into the mud only after a patch of sunlight crossed their pen. Earlier, when they'd been in the shade, they had stood dry by the fence. It wasn't about being dirty. It was about the heat.

"Watch their pen," she told Nadine. "When the shade comes back, see if they get out."

They waited, sharing the last of Alexandra's crackers at their leisure while visitors drifted past. When the sun moved off the pen, the larger pig hauled itself up, crossed to the dry straw, and shook. The smaller one followed.

"They're using the mud like a pool," Sadie said. "The sign says pigs have very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water on hot days to cool off."

"Huh," said Nadine. "So the mud isn't the point."

"Right. Cooling off is the point."

Mr. Popescu clapped his hands for the group. "When we get back, each of you will summarize one thing you observed today," he said. "Make your claim explicit. Tell me exactly what you saw and what you concluded."

Sadie wrote one sentence in her notebook, then read it over. In the pen, the sunlight crept back across the mud, and the smaller pig lifted its head, watching the bright patch move.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
story:
The dinner table was tranquil, just the clink of forks and his dad scrolling his phone through box scores, when Elliot decided to bring it up. "Dad, do you think Bruno Reese is a bad hitter?"

"Average says he is," his dad said without looking up. "Two-fifty. That's the number."

Elliot's stomach tightened. He had spent all of recess arguing with Leonie and Sacha about this, and he had lost, badly. He flashed back to the blacktop, Sacha waving a printed stat sheet in his face, Leonie saying, "Face it, Elliot, two-fifty is two-fifty. The guy makes outs." Elliot had gone home quiet, but something about the number had nagged at him all afternoon, the way a pebble in a shoe seems small until you walk on it.

"Can I see your phone?" he asked now. His dad handed it over, and Elliot found Reese's page. Batting average, at-bats, hits, all lined up in cold columns. Then a separate column, far down the list, and Elliot's breath caught. Walks: one hundred and four. He counted them twice with his finger on the screen.

"Look at this," he said, sliding the phone across the mashed potatoes.

"A hundred and four walks," his dad read. "So?"

"So walks don't count as at-bats," Elliot said. "A batting average is just hits divided by at-bats, and a walk isn't an at-bat. Every single one of those hundred and four times he got on base, the average gives him nothing. Zero credit. It's like the number insulates you from half the story." He grabbed the sugar bowl and a handful of dried beans from the counter, laying them along the table edge. "These beans are his hits. These sugar packets are his walks. Now take away the packets." He swept them into his palm. "What's left is all the average can see."

His dad was quiet for a long moment, scrolling slowly. He put down his fork. He rubbed his jaw and looked at the little line of beans like it might change on him.

"Huh," he said. "From that perspective, he's on base more than half the time."

"Leonie's going to eat her words at recess tomorrow," Elliot said, scooping the beans into his pocket.

"Bring the stat sheet," his dad said. "I want to see her face."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Astigmatism happens when the cornea or lens is slightly egg-shaped, curving more in one direction than the other, which blurs vision at any distance.
story:
Brielle sat in the exam chair and read the letters on the far wall. The big E was easy, but the second line smeared sideways, as if someone had dragged a thumb through wet ink. Ms. Diallo flipped lenses into the frame in front of Brielle's eyes, one click at a time.

"Try this," Ms. Diallo said. "Better or worse?"

"Better. The F has a tail again." Brielle squinted at the card Ms. Diallo held up close, at arm's length. Those letters smeared too. That was the part she couldn't figure out. She had hypothesized that she was nearsighted like her dad, because nearsighted meant far things blurred. But if that were true, the near card should have been sharp, and it wasn't. So that idea was wrong.

She turned her head and found a poster beside the sink, a cross-section of an eye with the cornea drawn in. The cornea on the poster wasn't round like a ball. It was egg-shaped, curving more in one direction than the other, and a caption under it said this blurred vision at any distance. Any distance. That matched exactly what she'd noticed: smeared letters near and smeared letters far.

"That's it," Brielle said. "Mine's egg-shaped, curving more one way than the other. Is that called astigmatism?"

"That's what it's called," Ms. Diallo said, clicking in another lens. "Read the line for me."

Brielle read down to the tiny bottom row, every letter crisp and separate, and grinned at the mirror on the wall because now she could see her own grin. She felt optimistic about Monday, when she would pick up the real glasses. On the way out she stopped at the water cooler in the waiting room, pressed the valve for cold water, and drank while staring across the room at the eye chart hanging there. Even the smallest line held still.

"Those letters aren't going anywhere," she said.

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: When the Nile flood went down, it left a layer of dark, fertile mud on the fields, which is why Egyptians called their land Kemet, the black land.
story:
Logan slid the book back and pulled out another one. He had promised Ms. Dela Cruz his presentation would answer two things: why the ancient Egyptians built the pyramids, and how the Nile shaped their farming. So far every book showed pictures of the pyramids but explained them about as well as a postcard of a sandwich explains lunch.

"Dead end?" Lux asked, dropping into the chair across from him with a granola bar and zero sympathy.

"Every book says 'amazing engineering,'" Logan said. "Thanks. Very helpful. But why there? Why that spot, why that shape, why bother?" He tapped the page. "And the farming part is worse. It just says the Nile flooded every year. Floods destroy things. My uncle's basement proves that."

Lux chewed for a second. "Okay, weird connection time. My grandpa gardens, and he made me monitor his tomato pots all summer, like a tiny scientist. The pot with the darkest soil went completely bananas. Twice as many tomatoes. The pale dirt pot was a sad little graveyard." She pointed her granola bar at him. "Dirt that's dark is dirt that's loaded. You're welcome."

Logan stared at her. "Dark soil. The flood." He yanked the atlas over and found the Nile, running like a green thread through all that yellow desert. "So the flood isn't the disaster part. The disaster part is when it goes down. And when it goes down, it leaves a layer of dark, fertile mud on the fields." He flipped to the vocabulary page and his finger stopped on a word. "They called their land Kemet," he read out loud. "The black land."

"Sounds like a superhero," said Lux.

"Sounds like the answer." Logan grabbed a blank sheet and started sketching: fat harvests feeding whole cities of workers, farms strung along the river, pharaohs stacking a stone mountain on the black land's edge as a giant billboard of power. Brianna leaned over from the next table, snagged his pencil, and drew a tiny rat on the grain pile. "That's a parasite," she said. "Free of charge."

"That's a rat, and I love it." Logan laughed and kept writing, feeling optimistic for the first time all week. He raised his hand. "Ms. Dela Cruz? Can we have the projector Thursday? I've got a flood, some very good mud, and a rat."

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: Collecting money on Free Parking in Monopoly is a common house rule, not one of the official rules, which is why players from different homes argue about it.
story:
Jaxon set the Monopoly board on the dinner table between the lasagna and the salad bowl, because tonight Deanna and Kendra were staying for family dinner and game night. His dad cleared the plates, and his little brother pulled up a chair, already reaching for the car token.

Everything went fine until Deanna rolled a five and landed on Free Parking. "Yes," she said, rubbing her hands together. "Payday." She reached for the middle of the board, where Jaxon's family kept nothing at all.

"There's no money there," Jaxon said.

"Because you haven't been putting taxes in. I'll take what's owed from the bank, then."

"That's not how it works. Free Parking does nothing. It's just a free space."

Deanna folded her arms. "At my house, whoever lands on it gets the whole pot. Everybody plays that way."

Kendra looked between them. "At my house too. My cousin won once with like five hundred dollars from Free Parking." Jaxon's little brother chimed in that at his friend's house, you got fifty dollars. Nobody, it seemed, could agree.

Jaxon was about to argue louder when he remembered something Ms. Bear, his neighbor, had said about chess disputes: name the problem before you fight about the answer. So he raised his hand like a referee. "Wait. Let's name the actual problem. I think the problem isn't that Deanna's greedy."

"Thanks a lot," said Deanna, but she half smiled.

"The problem is we learned the game at different houses. My family plays one way, your families play another, and nobody ever said it out loud." He fetch the rulebook from the box and flipped to the page about Free Parking while everyone ate the last of the garlic bread. He ran his finger down the text. "See? Officially, Free Parking is just a rest space. The money thing is a house rule. A really common one, but a house rule."

Deanna leaned over and read it herself. "Huh. My dad taught me that. I thought it was a real rule." She seemed almost relieved, as though being wrong was better than being cheated.

"So here's my idea," Jaxon said. "We can't be immune to house rules just by reading the book, because they're fun and lots of families like them. So let's agree on one before we keep playing. We take a vote, majority wins, and nobody argues after that. That way there's no contradiction later when someone lands on it."

They voted. Three to two, they put the luxury tax and income tax payments into the middle, and whoever landed on Free Parking collected the pile. Deanna offered to let his little brother hold the pot so he would feel included even though he kept rolling threes.

"Good call," Kendra said quietly to Jaxon, and she convey her meaning with a fist bump under the table.

On Deanna's next turn, she rolled a five again and landed on Free Parking once more. His little brother slid the pile of bills across the board with both hands. "Payday," he announced.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Animals that eat only producers are called primary consumers, and the animals that eat them are called secondary consumers.
story:
Aubrey crouched on the patio with her chalk, drawing the biggest arrow she could manage, from the sun down to a patch of grass. "Science homework," she told Lucie, who had climbed over the fence the way she always did. "I have to draw a whole food chain, from the sun all the way to a top predator, and then explain what happens if one link disappears." The backyard was a good place for it, she figured. The sun was right there, warming the stones. Near the fence, the little solar lamps were still blinking off, their voltage drained from the night, which reminded her that everything out here started with sunlight. Even the maple leaves she'd raked into a pile last week were beginning to decompose into dark crumbs, going back into the dirt.

She drew the chain across the concrete: sun, then grass, then a caterpillar munching the grass, then a bird, then a hawk at the very top. Lucie frowned at it. "Okay, but Ms. Reddy said you have to use the right words." Aubrey flipped through her notebook until she found the page she'd copied off the board. "Animals that eat only producers are called primary consumers," she read. "That's the caterpillar. Producers are the plants." She tapped the bird. "And the animals that eat them are secondary consumers." Lucie picked up the blue chalk and wrote PRIMARY in wobbly letters over the caterpillar, then SECONDARY over the bird.

"Fine," Lucie said, "but the last part of the assignment is the part you're avoiding." Aubrey knew she was right. She hadn't written a single thing about what happened when a link disappeared, because she wasn't sure. She had a guess, though, and guesses could be tested. "Watch," she said. She wet her sleeve in the wading pool and scrubbed the grass off the patio. No grass. She looked at the caterpillar. No grass meant nothing for the caterpillar to eat, so it would starve or crawl away. No caterpillar, and the bird went hungry too. No birds, and the hawk would have to hunt somewhere else entirely. It went all the way up, like knocking over the first domino in a line.

"Wait," Lucie said slowly, pointing at the bird. "Then the hawk doesn't just lose the bird. It loses everything underneath it, all the way down." Aubrey grabbed her notebook and wrote it out, fast, before she could forget the shape of the idea. Then she redrew the grass, green and tall, right back where it belonged.

At the kitchen door, her mom called that dinner was ready. "Coming," Aubrey shouted, and drew one last arrow, from the hawk straight back down toward the sun.

activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
knowledge_domain: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
fact: A waxing Moon's lit part is growing night by night, and a waning Moon's lit part is shrinking.
story:
Lauren had one problem bigger than her notorious locker, which had swallowed three assignments already. Last night her two cousins had argued in the group chat until midnight. One swore the Moon was getting bigger this week, the other said it was shrinking, and both had demanded that Lauren, the science person of the family, settle it. She had typed "idk" and felt it like a stone in her shoe.

At lunch she negotiated with Lyndon for half his pudding, promising him the last word in any argument for a whole day. Magnus just came along because he liked lamps. They carried Mr. Ba's desk lamp, a volleyball, and a marble into the empty art room, and Lauren made one quick adaptation to the plan: she taped the marble to the top of the volleyball, so the marble was the Moon and the volleyball was Earth, and the lamp could stand in for the Sun by the window.

"You're on Earth," she told Magnus, bending him down so his eye hovered above the marble. "Tell me what you see."

"A dark ball," Magnus reported. Then she walked the marble around the volleyball, slowly, the way the real Moon crawls around the real Earth. "Wait. There's a sliver now. Like a fingernail clipping."

"Keep going." Lauren moved it a quarter turn, then half.

"It's filling up," Magnus said. "It's like a cookie getting un-bitten."

Lyndon, who had been sulking into his pudding, leaned in. "So it's growing. That means my cousin's right and yours is wrong, and mine owes me five dollars."

"Only if it's still going this way," Lauren said. She kept walking the marble around, and past the far side of the volleyball, Magnus called out that the cookie was being eaten again, sliver by sliver.

"Oh," Lyndon said, straightening up. "I want to change my answer. It depends on which part of the lap it's on."

Lauren grinned. "A Moon whose lit part is growing night by night is waxing," she said, "and when it's shrinking, it's waning." She pulled out her phone. "Now hold still, Magnus. I need a photo of you being the Earth."

"Best job I've had all week," said the Earth, and did not blink.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Mandarin Chinese puts a measure word between a number and a noun: "one cat" is "yì zhī māo," where "zhī" is the measure word used for many animals.
story:
At the cultural festival, Penelope pressed her nose against the tent flap and inhaled the smell of fried dumplings and sweet bean buns. Inside, a long table held paper lanterns, ink brushes, and a poster that said Learn a Sentence. A grandparent of one of her classmates, a woman with silver hair and a smile like a comma, was helping kids say things in Mandarin. Penelope wanted one thing: to record a full sentence about her family and her orange cat, Pumpkin, for the festival's video booth, which would play on the big screen at sunset. The line for the booth closed in twenty minutes.

She started strong. "Wǒ yǒu yì māo," she said into the microphone, meaning I have one cat. But when she checked the tablet's sample recording, the fluent speaker had said something different, with a strange extra syllable in the middle. Penelope played both clips again and again. Same meaning, different sound. She scribbled the two versions in her notebook. There had to be a pattern, some small piece her sentence was missing, and she intended to find it before the booth closed.

She grabbed her friend Bree, who was dragging Pierre-Olivier toward the dumpling stand, and marched them to the corner where the silver-haired grandmother was folding paper lanterns. "Could you listen to me say something?" Penelope asked. She tried her sentence slowly, and the grandmother gently added the missing little word, "zhī," right after the number. Penelope's ears went hot. The word sat between one and cat, exactly where the fluent recording had a syllable. She tested it, moving it like a puzzle piece. In front of the number it sounded wrong; after the noun it vanished into confusion. Only that one slot worked.

She raced back to the booth, weaving between a drum circle and a table of mango slices, and recorded fast: her mother, her father, her little brother, and Pumpkin. "Wǒ yǒu yì zhī māo," she said, and the volunteer's eyebrows lifted approvingly. At sunset she stood between Bree and Pierre-Olivier, sticky mango juice on her fingers, and watched her sentence transform into glowing characters on the giant screen. Mr. Diallo, her neighbor from two houses down, tapped her shoulder and pointed at the word in the middle of her cat sentence. "What's that little one?" he asked. Penelope grinned and said, "That's zhī. It goes between the number and the cat."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: U.S. food safety guidelines say poultry is safely cooked when its thickest part reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
story:
Colton held the thermometer like it was a magic wand and poked it into the chicken breast sizzling on the grill in his backyard. His parents were stuck at his little sister's dance recital across town, and he had promised them dinner would be ready by six. His friend Amar sat on the porch steps, guardedly optimistic.

"You're measuring chicken like a scientist," Amar said. "My uncle just cuts it open and looks."

"That's guessing," Colton said. He had looked it up an hour ago: U.S. food safety guidelines say poultry is safely cooked when its thickest part reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer. "Guessing is how you get chewy chicken, or worse. Watch."

He slid the thermometer into the thickest part of the biggest piece and waited. 151. Not done. He turned the heat down a little, because his mom had once told him rushed chicken burns outside and stays raw inside, and rushed anything usually turns out worse.

Amar wanted to try. He had been begging since they started, mostly because he liked gadgets with digital screens. "Can I check the next one? Please. I'll evaluate each piece super carefully."

"Fine, but push it into the middle of the thickest part, not the edge." Colton handed it over. "The edge cooks first, so it lies to you."

"That's a weird sentence," Amar said, but he did it right. 148, 149, then finally the screen blinked up: 166.

"Sixty-six?" Amar squinted. "In this context, is that good or terrible?"

"Fahrenheit, so it's good. Sixty-six Celsius would be a whole different chicken." Colton flipped the last piece onto the platter, and they stood over the steam, grinning like they had won something.

Headlights swept the fence. His mom called through the car window, "Is it edible?"

"Perfectly cooked," Colton announced, holding up the thermometer like a trophy. "One hundred sixty-six degrees, measured scientifically."

"Well, bring the science inside," she said. "I'm starving."

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: In a parallel circuit, each bulb has its own path to the battery, so the others stay lit if one bulb breaks.
story:
Evelyn pressed the third wire into place and held her breath. At the maker table in the science museum, her bulb had glowed twice already, and twice it had gone dead the moment Lamar nudged the project. Now the bulb sat dark again, and the demonstration started in ten minutes.

"Try it," said Ali, tapping the switch. Nothing happened. Evelyn frowned at the board. The battery was fine, the wires were fine, and she could not see the problem, whatever it was. That was the worst part. Electricity was invisible, and a broken connection looked exactly like a good one. She had learned that trick about light in the optics room downstairs, how a prism could refract a white beam into a rainbow, bending something you could not otherwise see. She needed a way to bend electricity into view.

Then Mr. Weber walked past with a jar of glowing moss, some kind of fungus from the forest exhibit, and Evelyn stared at the tiny lights inside it. Lots of separate little lights. Not one. "Wait," she said slowly. "What if it's one long path right now? One bulb, one path, and if anything breaks anywhere, everything goes dark." She pulled the wires apart and started over, giving the bulb its own pair of wires straight to the battery.

Her fingers were hesitant at first, because if she was wrong, they would have nothing at all. She clipped, tucked, and flipped the switch. The bulb lit. Then, on purpose, she unscrewed the bulb halfway, until it should have gone dead. It stayed glowing. She tightened it again and turned to the others.

"It's a parallel circuit," she said. "Each bulb has its own path to the battery, so if one bulb breaks, the others stay lit."

Lamar grabbed the second bulb and clicked it into place. "So even if I break one, the rest keep going." He turned to the exhibit table. "Mr. Weber, come watch this."

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: Orchestras tune to a concert A played by the oboe, because its pitch is steady and its penetrating sound is easy for everyone to hear.
story:
The dressing room smelled like dust and somebody's banana, which Zoya insisted was the most nutritious thing you could eat before a concert. Arianna held her violin under her chin without bowing it, because her hands were shaking too much to trust. In twenty minutes she would walk onto a stage for the first time in her life, and all she could think about was the strange thing she had noticed at the dress rehearsal: the whole orchestra had gone silent and waited for a single note from one small oboe.

"Why do we all wait for that one instrument?" Arianna asked. "Nobody waits for me."

Zoya, who played clarinet, shrugged. "Maybe the oboe's just bossy."

Arianna didn't buy that. She closed her eyes and replayed the rehearsal in her head. The oboe player had held out a steady tone, and every section had tuned to it, one after another. She remembered asking Ms. Fernando later, in the hallway, and Ms. Fernando had only said, "That's the concert A," and walked off with a cart of music stands, as if that settled everything. It hadn't settled anything. But Arianna had a theory, and she tested it right there in the dressing room. She played her open A string, then listened hard while Alec, who sat second chair oboe, played his. Her note wobbled against his, sharp, so she turned her fine tuner a tiny amount and played again. Closer. Another small turn. There. His sound was steady and it cut straight through the room, easy to hear even over five kids warming up at once.

"So that's it," she said, spine straightening even though her knees hadn't gotten the message. "The oboe's pitch is steady, and it's easy for everyone to hear. That's why the whole orchestra tunes to its A."

"Then cite your source," Zoya said, grinning. "Alec, play it again."

Alec lifted his oboe, and the note rang out through the dressing room door just as Ms. Fernando's voice came down the corridor: "Places, everyone!"

Arianna picked up her bow and said, "Let's go."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: A eulogy is a speech praising a person who has died; the word comes from Greek roots meaning to 'speak well of'.
story:
The synagogue smelled of old wood and someone's lavender perfume, and Ruby sat in the third row holding her folded speech so tightly the paper creased. Her grandmother had died nine days ago, and now everyone expected Ruby to stand up at the front and talk. "It's called a eulogy," her father had explained at the kitchen table. "From Greek roots. It means to speak well of someone." Ruby had thought that was a strange job for words, since she couldn't even say the word "Grandma" out loud yet without her throat going tight.

She had tried writing the speech five times. One version was three pages long and included the family tree, which even she found boring. One version was two sentences. The problem was picking just one memory, because how could one memory hold a whole grandmother? In the row behind her, Drew and Jett from school sat squeezed between their parents, both of them scrubbed and wearing collars they clearly hated. Drew leaned forward and whispered, "You okay? You look like you're solving a math problem." Ruby whispered back, "I'm trying to test a theory." She had decided that if she told the smallest memory she had, the one nobody else would even know was important, it might work better than the big impressive ones.

The rabbi nodded at her, and Ruby stood. Her shoes were quiet on the carpet, like the carpet had been designed exactly for nervous people. "My grandmother had a rule," she said, once she reached the podium. "If you were about to abandon a board game because you were losing, you had to finish it first. She said quitting was the only thing that actually made you lose." A small laugh moved through the rows of chairs. "One time we played checkers on her porch and a seagull, a huge predatory seagull with eyes like a tiny burglar, landed on the table and stole the red king piece. Grandma said that was the only anomaly in forty years of her checker career, and she made me write it down in a notebook she kept called Things That Happened."

Ruby looked out at all the faces, and her father was crying but smiling at the same time, which she hadn't known a face could do. "So that's my eulogy," she said. "I'm speaking well of her, like the word means. She was the person who made you finish the game, and she made even a seagull stealing a checker piece into a story worth keeping."

She walked back to her seat, and Drew slid over to make room. Jett passed her a tissue box even though she wasn't crying, which was somehow funny. "Good theory," Drew whispered. Ruby tucked the crumpled speech into her pocket. "Turns out you only need one checker piece," she whispered back.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: In the Scripps National Spelling Bee, a speller may start over, but changing any letters already said counts as a misspelling.
story:
The library meeting room smelled like old carpet and lemon polish, and the folding chairs had been arranged in two crooked rows for the spelling bee. Rose sat between Valentina and Dash, holding her word list so tightly the paper crinkled. The prize was a real trophy, small but golden, and Rose had wanted it since third grade, when she had gone out on the word "rhythm" and cried in the biography section.

Ms. Jean-Louis, the children's librarian, stood at the front desk with the official list of words. "Rules, one more time," she said. "You may ask for the definition, the language of origin, and a sentence. You may start a word over. But listen carefully, spellers. Starting over is allowed. Changing any letters you have already said counts as a misspelling." Rose nodded, though her mind was mostly on the trophy.

The early rounds were kind. Dash got "harbor" and spelled it slowly, like he was walking on ice. Valentina got "sapphire" and grinned after the bell didn't ring. Rose had "categorize," which she spelled without trouble, thinking how convenient it was that the hardest part was remembering the z. Two more rounds thinned the field until only Rose, Valentina, and a boy from another school remained.

Then came "vessel." Rose knew the word, and she knew what it meant; the sentence Ms. Jean-Louis read was about a ship, a vessel crossing the harbor. Rose began. "V. E." She paused. In her head she suddenly saw the other spelling, the one with only one s, and it looked right. The room was so quiet she could hear the clock above the returns desk. She could start over. She knew that. But starting over would not let her change anything, because the two e's were already out of her mouth, hanging in the air, and a different letter in that same spot would count as a misspelling. Whatever she said next had to build on what she had said, or repeat it exactly.

She said the rest carefully. "S. S. E. L." The pause before the final letter felt long enough for the clock to tick twice. Ms. Jean-Louis rang the small bell, the bright one that meant correct, and Valentina squeezed Rose's wrist from the seat behind her.

The boy from the other school went out on "camouflage," and Valentina went out on "bougainvillea," which Rose privately thought was an arbitrary choice for a library bee, like asking someone to spell a word from Mars. That left Rose alone at the front for the championship word.

"Mnemonic," said Ms. Jean-Louis. "It means something that helps you remember."

Rose almost laughed. She thought of her mother's trick, the sentence about eating a small treat after dinner, and she didn't even need it. "M. N. E. M. O. N. I. C. Mnemonic."

The bell rang, and Dash stood up on his folding chair and waved both arms. Ms. Jean-Louis handed Rose the little trophy, warm from sitting under the reading lamp. Valentina shouted, "Take a picture, take a picture," and Dash was already aiming the library's ancient camera.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Eid al-Fitr is the Muslim celebration marking the end of Ramadan, the month in which many Muslims fast from dawn until sunset.
story:
The long tables at the community hall were covered with food by four o'clock, but nobody was eating. Naomi stood with her plate and looked down the row of samosas, dates, and a big honey cake with white icing, and every adult she could see was holding a cup of tea and talking, hands nowhere near the serving spoons. Her little cousin tugged her sleeve and said he was hungry, and the cake was scheduled to be cut at six, which gave Naomi two hours to figure out what was going on before a room full of children started complaining.

Her first idea was that the food was for later, like a display at a bakery. She tested it by reaching for a samosa, and a woman near her shook her head and pointed at the clock above the stage. Naomi put the samosa back. Her second idea was worse: that nobody liked the food. She found her classmate Rachael by the punch bowl and asked why the feast was just sitting there.

"Because sunset hasn't come yet," Rachael said. "Today is Eid al-Fitr, the celebration at the end of Ramadan." She said the last day of the month still counted, and that during Ramadan, Muslims fast from dawn until sunset. "No food, no water, from sunrise to sundown, for a whole month," she said. "Tomorrow we can eat whenever we want. That's what Eid is for."

Naomi thought about that. She had woken at six that morning and eaten two bowls of cereal, and by noon she had been asking for crackers. A whole month of waiting until sunset, every single day, was hard to picture. From her cousin's perspective, missing one snack was a disaster. From Rachael's, tonight was the finish line of something that had lasted thirty days. He could manage another hour. Naomi found him a chair by the window instead of the food table, and told him to watch the sky with her, since the rule depended on the sun and not on the kitchen clock.

The question of which dessert should be served first became controversial when the honey cake and the baklava came out side by side, and a group of kids began arguing so loudly that a man in a gray jacket came over to settle it. Rachael's little brother insisted cake first because it could be cut faster. Rachael said that was unfair to everyone who had been waiting a month and that dates should go first, since that was how her family always broke the fast. Naomi, who had come in wanting cake more than anything, changed her mind and raised her hand for dates.

At 6:41 the sun slipped behind the roof of the building across the street, the waiting ceased, and the room filled with the sound of plates. Rachael pressed a date into Naomi's palm and grinned. "One month done. Try it."

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: A proposed law is called a bill until it passes all its stages; once it becomes law it is called an Act.
story:
Joshua stood on the courthouse steps with his class, holding the worksheet Mr. Teo had given them, and stared at question three: "Why does the sign say Act while our textbook calls it a bill?" Around him, students from three schools were filing inside for the Youth Legislature Day, where kids would pretend to pass a law about bike lanes.

"It's a typo," said Thiago, peering over his shoulder. "Just write typo."

Joshua didn't think it was a typo. Inside the chamber, he sat between Thiago and Issac, watching a real legislator explain the day's simulation. She kept saying the word bill. "Our bill goes to committee," she said. "Then the whole chamber votes on the bill." But the plaque on the wall honored the Safe Routes Act, and the paper on everyone's desk was titled Bicycle Safety Bill. Same topic, two names. Joshua turned his pencil over and over, feeling like the answer was hiding underneath something.

"Maybe they change the name on purpose," Issac whispered, "like a nickname."

"That's it," Joshua whispered back. He raised his hand, and when the legislator called on him, he asked, "So is it called a bill while it's still going through all the stages, and then it's called something else after?"

"Exactly," she said. "It's a bill until it passes all its stages; once it becomes law, it's an Act." She smiled like he'd unlocked a door.

Joshua wrote it down so fast his pencil tore the paper a little. During the simulation, their bill survived committee, survived debate, survived a vote that Issac nearly lost for them by voting no out of confusion. "Wait, we want yes," Issac said, changing his vote, and the room laughed. When the speaker declared the bill passed, the student clerk crossed out Bill on the sheet and wrote Act above it, and Joshua felt the whole process decompose in his mind into clear, stackable stages, each one visible at last.

Afterward, Thiago read Joshua's answer to question three. "Okay," he admitted, "not a typo. There's some irony in that, too. I was the one who told you to guess." Mr. Teo, gathering worksheets at the door, paused at their pages. "These two are the only ones who got it," he said, and tapped the plaque. Joshua looked up at the brass letters spelling Act, then down at his smudged sheet spelling bill.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be tested against evidence and shown to be true or false, while an opinion expresses a belief, feeling or judgment that evidence cannot prove.
story:
Alexis leaned over the bean plants on the back counter and counted leaves for the third time in five minutes, hoping more would appear. The science fair started in twenty minutes, and their display board had a hole in the middle of it where the conclusion was supposed to go.

"Mine says the beans near the window are the prettier plants," Annalise read off her notepad. "That fills the space, right?"

"Mr. Anderson said we need a conclusion that someone can actually check," Alexis said. She scrutinized the two pots, tilting her head to compare the seedlings. The window beans stood tall and crowded with leaves. The ones by the door were pale and slouching like they had given up on life.

April hurried over with a ruler in one hand and a half-eaten granola bar in the other. "I measured the tall ones twice. Sixteen centimeters on Monday, twenty-one today. The door ones only grew one centimeter."

"So," Annalise said slowly, "is pretty the thing he wants?"

Alexis turned a fresh notecard over and wrote two lines. "Look. Saying the fern in the corner is the prettiest plant in this room, that's an opinion. I can't test pretty. Nobody can measure it and find out if it's true or false. But saying the beans by the window grew faster, that's a claim we can check. We have the numbers right here."

Annalise squinted at the notecard. "So if someone said, no, the door beans grew faster, we could prove them wrong?"

"With the ruler," April said through a mouthful of granola bar. "The ruler never lies. Unlike my brother, who says my granola bars taste like cardboard. That's his opinion, and I have decided it cannot be tested."

Alexis laughed and copied the two lines onto the board in her best handwriting: the window beans grew from sixteen to twenty-one centimeters in four days, while the door beans grew one centimeter. Evidence, measured twice. Underneath, in smaller letters, she added that in her opinion the window beans were also the superior plants, but that part was just for fun.

Mr. Anderson began calling tables to the front, and the tranquil hum of the classroom sharpened into a scrape of chairs and chatter. Annalise grabbed the glue, April guarded the ruler like a dragon guarding gold, and Alexis pressed the conclusion onto the board with both hands just as their table was called.

"You three look pleased," Mr. Anderson said, stopping at their display.

"We had a whole reasoning breakthrough," April announced. "Also, you should try the granola bars. That part is an opinion, but it is a strong one."

He raised an eyebrow, picked up their data sheet, and started counting the leaves himself.

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: A note one octave higher than another vibrates exactly twice as fast, which is why the two sound like the same note at different heights.
story:
John stood in the corner of Mr. Popescu's studio, clutching his sheet music like a shield. The winter concert was in three weeks, and the choir had split into two groups for the first time. Jemma's group sang the high part. John's group sang the low one. Every time they tried singing together, John's ears got tangled and he drifted up to Jemma's notes like a duck following the wrong mother.

"You did it again," Jemma said after the third crash and burn. "You're copying me. It's like you're a mirror."

"I can't help it. Your part is louder in my head than mine."

Mr. Popescu played the two starting notes on the piano, one after the other, over and over. John closed his eyes and scrutinized the sound, hunting for the difference the way he hunted for his missing sock under the bed. The notes weren't the same, exactly. But they felt like twins, one tall and one short, like an emperor standing beside a kneeling servant who was somehow the same person.

"Wait," John said. "Play those two again." He hummed the low note, then the high one. "They're the same note. Just one is... upstairs."

"An octave," Mr. Popescu said. "A note one octave higher vibrates exactly twice as fast."

"Twice as fast? So my note is lazy and Jemma's is hyper?"

"Basically," Jemma said, delighted.

That was the key. If Jemma's note was his note running at double speed, then it was family, not a stranger, and his ears stopped panicking. He tested it, humming his low note while she sang hers above him. They locked together like train wheels on a track.

At the concert, the two groups blended so smoothly that a kid in the front row whispered that harmonies were "controversial," because they sounded too good to be legal. John just grinned and held his part, steady as a stone at the bottom of a river.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: The independent variable is the one thing an experimenter changes on purpose to see what happens.
story:
Emmett balanced two paper airplanes on the kitchen counter and frowned at them. One had wings bent up at the tips, the other had flat wings, and the flat one was made from the slick paper from a cereal box while the bent one was plain notebook paper. He had thrown each three times down the hallway, and the bent one had glided every single time, but he couldn't say why.

"Maybe it's the fancy paper," Flora said, watching from the stool while she ate crackers. "Maybe the bendy wings do nothing."

"But which one is it?" Emmett flipped the flat-wing plane over. "What if I made one plane with the bendy wings AND the slick paper? Then if it flew, would that disclose which part was doing the work?"

Flora chewed slowly. "It flew before with bendy wings and it flew before with slick paper. If the new one flies, it could still be either one winning."

Emmett set the plane down. She was right, and it annoyed him pleasantly, the way a puzzle annoys you when it starts to open up. "So what if I keep everything the same except one thing? Same paper, same creases, and I only change the wing bend. Then whatever happens has to be because of the bend."

Ms. Zhao, his neighbour, had drifted in through the back door to borrow sugar and was now watching with her mug of tea. "When I ran the science fair," she said mildly, "we had a monopoly on arguments about exactly this. One boy changed his recipe and his oven at the same time and couldn't tell which one made his cake rise."

"So change only one thing," Emmett said.

"On purpose," Ms. Zhao said. "The one thing an experimenter changes on purpose to see what happens. Mine made that rule mandatory before anyone could touch the materials table."

Emmett folded two fresh planes from identical notebook paper, identical creases, identical everything except the wing tips, one bent up, one flat. He threw the bent one down the hallway and it curved in a slow, beautiful arc and landed on the couch. He threw the flat one and it nosedived into the shoe rack.

"Bendy wings win," Flora announced, crumbs on her chin.

"For notebook paper," Emmett said, already reaching for the slick cereal box. "I wonder if slick paper wins with flat wings." He creased a new fold and held it up to the light.

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: A scary story can set off a real fear response, with a racing heart and faster breathing, even when the listener knows it is made up.
story:
Anais had never slept anywhere but her cousin Thierry's house before, and even there she had always gone home by nine. Now she was staying the whole night, and Linkin, who lived on the same street, had been allowed to join. Thierry's mom had made popcorn and then left them with sleeping bags in the den, where the only light came from the fish tank.

"Tell the one about the lighthouse keeper," Linkin said, and Thierry did, lowering his voice until the last part, which was about a hand on a stair rail in the dark. Anais noticed her own heart banging and her breath going quick and shallow, which puzzled her, because she knew Thierry made the story up on the spot. He had done the same thing last summer at the lake, and she had laughed then. She was still trying to deduce why her body believed him when her brain did not when the stairs creaked for real.

Thierry shot straight up like a spring and yelped. The cat, huge and gray, strolled into the den, sat on Linkin's sleeping bag, and began washing one paw. Thierry laughed, but his hand was still pressed flat against his chest. "It's the story," Anais said, sitting forward. "Your body doesn't care that you made it up. It heard a scary thing in the dark and got ready to run, so a creak on the stairs set you off like a fire alarm." She thought of herself at the lake, insisting she wasn't scared while her heart hammered, and how she had decided then that being frightened meant being weak. Maybe she had been unfair to herself. Her mind had known better all along; her body just hadn't been consulted.

"Prove it," Thierry said. "Tell one yourself, and we'll see if I'm the only one." Anais made her voice slow and quiet, the way the storyteller at her mother's office party had done, an assertive, steady voice that made everyone lean in even though the story was only about a lost dog. By the time she reached the part about the doorknob turning, Linkin's popcorn was scattered across the floor and Thierry was holding the cat like a shield.

"Okay," Thierry whispered. "Point taken." The doorknob turned for real, and all three of them screamed before the cat wriggled free and bolted for the door.

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: Scratch is named after DJ scratching, where a record is moved back and forth on a turntable to remix sounds.
story:
Simon sat at Grandpa's kitchen table with the old laptop, building a game where an emperor penguin dodged a predatory shark that patrolled the ice. The shark moved in a loop, and an if-then block added a point to the score every time the penguin reached a fish. The score was the problem. Every time the penguin touched a fish, the counter jumped by fifty instead of one.

He told himself the code could not be lying. The computer did exactly what the blocks said, so something he could not see had to be making the block run again and again. His first idea was that the fish was too big, so the penguin touched it for many frames in a row. He shrank the fish sprite, but the score still jumped. Then he opened the loop that moved the fish back to its start position and found the score block sitting inside it, running once for every repeat. He dragged it out onto the main stack, and the score ticked up by exactly one.

He wanted sound next, a little chirp for every point. While hunting through the sound library he found a folder of record-scratches, and next to it a note on the website. He read it twice, then spun around in his chair. "Grandpa, did you know Scratch is named after DJ scratching? Like moving a record back and forth on a turntable to remix sounds."

Grandpa set down his coffee. "That I did not know. But I've got a turntable downstairs, if you want to hear the real thing."

In the basement, Grandpa pulled a record from its sleeve. One wire had gone frayed, so they wrapped it with electrical tape first to insulate it, then Grandpa lowered the needle. He nudged the record backward, let it slip forward, caught it again. Simon recorded five seconds of it on the laptop.

"Watch this," he said, and dropped the sound into the game. Every time the score went up, the penguin chirped and the record scratched. Grandpa leaned in close to the speaker. "Play it again."

activity: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
knowledge_domain: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
fact: For long stretches, the Rhine and Danube rivers formed the Roman Empire's northern border in Europe, with forts and soldiers posted along their banks.
story:
Isaac spread the giant map of the Roman Empire across his bedroom floor, weighting the corners with a shoe, a hockey puck, and a suspicious orange from lunch. Tomorrow he had to stand up in Ms. Grewal's class and explain, using the map, why the empire split and fell, and so far his big discovery was that ancient borders were wriggly.

His phone buzzed. A text from Seth: "Don't panic but I heard Ms. Grewal says if you just point at the map and say 'it was big' she will fake her own death on the spot. Do NOT be that guy."

"Help me then," Isaac texted back, and sent a photo of the map.

Seth's reply came fast. "WAIT. Look at the top. The border wiggles along two blue lines all the way across. Why would a border do that? Borders are usually straight like my haircut."

Isaac flopped down and traced the frontier with his finger, half expecting the orange to obstruct his view. It did. He shoved it aside. The northern border ran along one blue squiggle, then another, stretching across the whole map. He checked the map key. Rivers. The Rhine and the Danube. Of course. Rivers were like walls nature had already built.

"So picture this," Isaac said out loud to his poster of a shark, rehearsing. "The Rhine and Danube rivers formed the northern border in Europe, with forts and soldiers posted along their banks." The shark looked skeptical, so Isaac tried again, pointing at invisible classmates. "Rome couldn't just expand forever past the rivers, because the whole edge needed soldiers, and soldiers cost money, and money was the corrosive stuff eating the empire from inside. Too much border, not enough empire." He grinned. "Too much empire, not enough everything."

The phone buzzed one more time: "Found my thing. I'm doing the part where it split in two. You can have rivers. Rivers are the boring half."

"Boring?" Isaac picked up the orange and held it like a microphone. "Rivers are the whole signal, Seth. Get over here and bring snacks."

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: In German, every noun begins with a capital letter, so "I have a dog and a cat" is written "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze."
story:
The cultural festival had filled the gym with folding tables, and Florence had claimed one near the fan-shaped windows to finish her German poster. Her draft read "Ich habe einen hund und eine katze," and the laptop's spell-checker had underlined two words in wobbling red. She stared at it. Why would "hund" and "katze" be wrong when they were definitely spelled right? She checked the dictionary app, and there they sat: Hund, Katze, both with capitals.

"Your computer is broken," said Quintin, leaning over her shoulder.

"It's not broken. Look, it flagged every single noun." Florence tapped the screen. "Hund, Katze, Bruder, Mutter, all of them." She scrolled down her sentence about her family, watching the red squiggles line up under each noun and skip the other words entirely. It was a pattern, like footprints. Could it be a rule? She typed "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze," and the squiggles vanished, one by one.

"So every noun starts with a capital?" asked Johnathan, who had drifted over from the origami table with a transparent plastic bag of paper cranes. "Even in the middle of a sentence?"

"That's what it looks like." Florence tried it on "Ich habe einen Bruder," and no red appeared. "The spell-checker was trying to tell me, and I despised it for nothing. All those times I clicked ignore."

Mr. Zhou, who was running the dumpling stall two tables down and spoke six languages, paused beside them. "In German, every noun begins with a capital letter," he said, and moved on with his tray.

Florence rewrote the whole poster, feeling the irony of it: the tool she'd been fighting had been her best teacher all along. She held up the finished sentence for Quintin and Johnathan to see. "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze," she read aloud, and every noun stood tall.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In 1972 James Woodward proposed writing 'Deaf' with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase 'deaf' for the hearing condition itself.
story:
Elena stood in Dominique's kitchen with markers spread across the table like a rainbow that had exploded. The poster board in front of them was for Dominique's sign-language club, and so far it said WELCOME TO THE DEAF CLUB in big blue letters, except Elena had written "deaf" with a lowercase d, and Dominique kept frowning at it.

"You spelled it wrong," Dominique said, tapping the word.

"I definitely didn't," Elena said. "D-E-A-F. I can spell, thank you very much."

"Not the letters. The capital." Dominique flipped her laptop around and slid it across the table. "Look. My club leader told us. In 1972, James Woodward proposed writing Deaf with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase deaf for the hearing condition itself."

Elena leaned over the screen, close enough to smell the lemon cleaner on the table. The words stared back at her, and she felt that little flip in her stomach that happened when something she'd always seen one way suddenly had a second shape. So the same word could mean two different things depending on nothing but a capital letter? A whole culture hiding inside one small piece of punctuation? She wondered how many other words were secretly doing that, walking around in disguise.

"That's like a secret code," she said slowly. "The word looks the same, but if you know the rule, you know exactly what somebody means." She picked up the blue marker and began to fix the D, and her palm started to perspire against the plastic, so she switched hands.

Dominique's little brother, Junior, thundered into the kitchen, grabbed a red marker, and drew what he claimed was a mountain. "It's a plateau," he announced. "Flat on top. Very famous."

"That is approximately a potato," Elena said, and Dominique laughed so hard she knocked over a cup of pencils.

They worked until the poster glowed with the big corrected word and a border of hands signing the alphabet. Junior added his potato-plateau in one corner, and somehow it looked right. Dominique held the poster up against the refrigerator, squinting.

"So when people see the capital D," Elena said, "they'll know it's about people and culture, not just ears."

"Exactly," Dominique said. She signed something quick and fluid, her hands moving like they were telling a joke.

"What was that?"

"Poster looks awesome," Dominique translated. Then she signed it again, slower, and pointed at Elena's hands. "Your turn."

Elena's fingers fumbled through the shapes, wrong twice, closer the third time, and Junior clapped like she had scored a goal.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard modern piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
Cameron pressed one key after another on the classroom piano, listening for the note that had been driving him crazy all week. His audition for the youth orchestra was in six days, and if he earned a scholarship, his lessons would be free. But every time he played his piece, one spot sounded wrong, sour in a way he could hear but not see.

Isa slid onto the bench beside him. "Still the same measure?"

"Still the same," Cameron said. He played the measure again, and the bad note buzzed in his ears like a trapped fly. "I'm hitting the right key, I think. So why does it sound wrong?" He stared at the keyboard, all those white and black rows, and an idea came to him. Maybe he was hitting a black key when he meant to hit a white one, or the other way around. He could not see his fingers clearly when he played fast. So he would test it. He played the measure slowly, watching, and found his thumb landing on a black key instead of the white one next to it.

"There," he said. "That's it."

Isa grinned. "You know, my grandpa has a piano like this. I counted the keys once because I didn't believe him. Fifty-two white and thirty-six black. Eighty-eight in all."

Cameron looked down the whole length of the keyboard. "Eighty-eight chances to hit the wrong one," he said, and they both laughed. "But only one I need to fix."

Benedict called from across the room, where he was putting away his trumpet. "Ms. Kovalenko says five more minutes!"

Cameron played the measure ten more times, slowly, then at full speed. The sour buzz was gone, and the line came out clean and warm, like sunlight through the practice room window. It was not the whole piece, and his audition was still a long shot, but it was an approximate version of the thing he wanted, and it was closer than yesterday. He could work with closer.

Isa nudged him. "Again?"

Cameron set his fingers on the keys and began the piece from the top.

activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
knowledge_domain: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
fact: At new moon, the Moon lies roughly between Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us and it looks dark.
story:
Last Tuesday night, Noah could not find the Moon anywhere. He stood on the back step with his dad, scanning the sky from the fence to the oak tree, and it simply was not there. "It vanished," Noah said. "Moons don't vanish," his dad said, but he could not say where it had gone either. That became Noah's problem, and it was still bugging him at school the next morning.

He grabbed Loic near the lockers. "If the Moon is always up there somewhere, why couldn't we see it at all?" Loic shrugged, so Noah wrote the question on a sticky note and stuck it to his binder. He wanted an answer he could actually point to, not just a sentence from a book.

In science, Ms. Okonkwo had set out a task: illustrate the Moon's phases for the class using the lamp on her desk and a white foam ball. Noah's group got Ilya too, and the three of them pushed their desks together. Noah held the ball at arm's length and walked a slow circle around Loic, who sat in the chair playing Earth. Halfway around, Noah stopped.

"Wait. Look at this." The lamp lit the side of the ball facing away from Loic. From Loic's chair, the ball showed only its dark, unlit face, a grey circle against the grey wall. "It's invisible from your seat," Noah said. "The lamp's over there, so the bright side is pointing away from you." Ilya leaned in and squinted. "So if the real Moon is between us and the Sun, its lit side faces away from us, and it looks dark from Earth. We wouldn't see anything." Loic turned in the chair. "Then where's my Moon? Gone."

Nooh checked the sticky note on his binder. "At new moon," he read slowly, working it out, "the Moon lies roughly between Earth and the Sun. That's the night we had. It didn't vanish, it was just turned dark side to us." The missing Moon stopped feeling like an anomaly, some freak event in the sky, and started feeling like a rule he could test. He walked the ball around Loic twice more, watching the lit slice grow and shrink.

Ms. Okonkwo came by as they labelled their diagram, and she did not correct a single arrow. "One kid in my last class said the Moon was endangered because it kept disappearing," she said, smiling. "You three won't be making that mistake." That night, Noah stood on the back step again with his dad and pointed at the thin curve of light low in the sky. "It's coming back around," he said. "Give it a few more nights and you'll see the whole bright face."

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Fractions can only be added directly when their denominators match, because the denominator names the size of the pieces being counted.
story:
The math club room smelled like the leftover brownies Helen had brought for the snack table, and Helen was guarding them like treasure. "Entry fee," she said, sliding the plate toward the middle of the table. "One solved problem per brownie. I need to defend my reputation around here."

Alexandra looked at her worksheet. "One half plus one third." She wrote an answer fast: two fifths. It looked right. One plus one, two plus three.

Keziah leaned over. "Try it with the fraction tiles. Actually move them."

Alexandra dug through the box of red and blue plastic pieces. She set out a half tile, then a third tile, and squinted at them. They were different sizes. Obviously different. She pushed them side by side and the two-fifths tiles she'd counted out sat there, matching nothing. Her answer had treated the pieces as if they were the same, and they weren't.

She sat back. It was like the flour at her grandmother's house last summer. The measuring cup had a line for a half and a line for a third, and when she'd poured them both into the bowl, her grandmother had asked how much she had so far. Alexandra had said two fifths of a cup, and her grandmother had laughed, not meanly, and said count the marks. The lines on the cup between a half and a third didn't match up either. The pieces were different sizes, so you couldn't just count them together.

Back at the table, Alexandra hunted through the tile box for pieces that would make both stacks match. Sixths worked. The half tile equaled three sixths. The third tile equaled two sixths. She snapped them together, counted, and wrote: five sixths.

"That's what I got," Keziah said. "The bottom number has to match before you can add."

Mr. Reddy walked past and dropped a new problem on their table, face down. "Only one rule on that one," he said. "Show me the pieces."

Alexandra flipped it over. One half minus one third. She was already reaching for the sixths.

"That one's mine too," Helen said, pulling her chair over. "Two brownies says you're faster than me."

"You're on." Alexandra laid out the tiles.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The Stanley Cup was donated by Lord Stanley, Canada's governor general, in 1892 and first awarded in 1893, making it the oldest trophy in North American professional sports.
story:
The living room was so crowded that Tyler had to sit on the floor between the couch and the coffee table, balancing his plate of nachos on his knees. The big game was tied with ten minutes left, and every save made the whole room groan or cheer at once. But Tyler kept noticing something else. When the camera showed the trophy waiting at rinkside, it looked battered and strange, dented all over, like somebody had dropped it down a staircase. His uncle kept saying it looked older than the team itself, and Cory, sprawled on the rug beside him, announced that the league probably just bought a cheap one and beat it up on purpose so it would seem legendary.

Tyler didn't believe that. "Trophies don't fake age," he said. "There has to be a real reason it looks like that." Cory grinned and folded his arms like a lawyer in a movie. "Fine, defendant," he said, "the court of this living room finds you guilty of making things up unless you can prove it." Tyler looked around the room. On the shelf behind the TV, between his mom's old novels, stood the family encyclopedia, the letter S volume. He remembered seeing hockey in it once. He stood up, wobbled past Naya's knees, and pulled it down while the crowd yelled at a near miss behind him.

The pages of tiny print were tedious to search, and he skipped whole sections about Saskatchewan and satellites before he found hockey. His finger ran down the column. There it was. "Listen," he said, and the room actually quieted a little, because the period had gone to intermission. "The trophy was donated by Lord Stanley, who was Canada's governor general, in 1892, and it was first awarded in 1893. That makes it the oldest trophy in North American professional sports." Naya sat up straight. "Older than football's?" "Older than all of them," Tyler said, and he checked twice to make sure the numbers matched before he closed the book.

"So it's beat up because it's actually ancient," Naya said. "Not because somebody sanded it in a garage." Cory sighed and handed Tyler the last nacho, which in their court clearly meant he lost the case. On the screen the third period was starting, and Tyler scooted back to his spot just as the puck dropped. "Come on," he said, pointing at the battered old cup gleaming in the lights. "You've been waiting longer than any of us."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
story:
Olivier stood at the long jump pit behind the gym, holding the clipboard that Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya had left with him while she went to supervise the shot put. His job was to write down every jump in the boys' qualifying category, and the list was getting messy. Timothe had jumped 4.20 meters, then 4.22, then fouled twice. Sacha had one legal jump of 4.25 and kept checking the clipboard over Olivier's shoulder like it might change.

"If I'm second, I make the final," Sacha said. "Fourth, I don't."

"Right now you're first," Olivier said, tapping the page.

Then Timothe walked to the board, ran, and landed at 4.26. One centimeter past Sacha. Sacha's shoulders dropped, and Olivier saw him do the math in his head: second place, final spot still safe, but barely.

Olivier looked at the list again. Timothe 4.26. Sacha 4.25. Two boys, one centimeter, and a ranking that said first and second as if the gap were some fixed thing. He remembered watching the hundred-meter final on TV with his dad last summer, when the silver medalist lost by less than a blink. His dad had said, "Imagine if they'd both been a hundredth slower. Same race, same runners, but the picture would look identical and nobody would know." Olivier had thought about that for days. A ranking shows order but not distance. Timothe could be ahead by one centimeter or by half a meter, and the results sheet would say exactly the same thing.

He tried an idea. "Sacha, you've got one jump left. Instead of just going safe, mark your takeoff a shoe-width back from the board."

"That wastes distance."

"You've fouled zero times, but you keep scraping the board," Olivier said. "One centimeter behind is the same as one centimeter fouled. Both mean second place. But one centimeter in front of the board, and the jump counts."

Sacha stared at the pit, then at his shoes, translucent tape still clinging to the left one from last week's blister. He walked back a shoe-width, ran, hit the board clean, and flew. Olivier leaned over the tape measure and felt his own heart thump. 4.31.

When Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya returned, she read the sheet. "New leader. By six centimeters." Sacha grinned and held up his hand, and Olivier slapped it.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: Many shelf labels show a unit price, such as the price per litre, so different sizes can be compared; the bigger carton is often, but not always, cheaper per litre.
story:
Mya had walked past the corner store a hundred times, but always with an adult holding the door. Today her mother had handed her a ten-dollar bill and a list with one word on it: milk. The laundromat sat halfway there, and Mya timed herself by it, counting the dryers in the window like checkpoints on a race course.

She was almost at the store when she spotted Freya coming out with a slushie, and they walked back in together. The milk cooler had two options. A big two-litre carton sat on the top shelf, and beside it, smaller one-litre cartons were stacked in a pyramid. Mya had enough money for either one, she realized, but not for both without checking her change.

"That one," Freya said, pointing at the pyramid. "Two small ones. More is more."

Mya was hesitant. She remembered last summer, when she had bought the big bag of popcorn at the pool and it had turned out to cost more than two small bags, which had seemed unfair in a way she couldn't explain at the time. Something about sizes and prices didn't always work the way you expected. She leaned closer to the shelf tag under the big carton and found a second, smaller number printed there.

"It says the price per litre," she read slowly. "Like a secret number for comparing." The big carton's per-litre price was lower than the small carton's. So the big carton was cheaper per litre, even though it cost more overall. She did the arithmetic on her palm with a pencil stub, wincing when the numbers wobbled, then checked again. Two small cartons would cost more than one big one, and she'd get the same amount of milk.

"Fine," Freya said, watching the cashier ring it up. "But you've carried it the whole way home. That thing has, like, no stamina."

"I have stamina," Mya said. "The milk just doesn't."
