The cashier counted the change into her hand, and Mya counted it again on the counter, coin by coin, matching it to the receipt. Exact. On the walk back, the carton got heavier with every block, and she stopped at the laundromat to shift it to her other arm. Through the window she could see Mr. Johansson folding towels, and he gave her a thumbs-up when she lifted the carton like a trophy.

Her mother was waiting on the steps. "Right change?"

"Right change," Mya said, "and right milk. The big one was cheaper per litre." She set it down on the step and shook out her aching fingers. "Next time, I'm bringing a wagon."

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, given on November 19, 1863, was about 272 words long and took roughly two minutes to deliver.
story:
Harrison stood at the kitchen counter with his speech outline spread in front of him and a timer on his mom's phone. Mr. Hoang had assigned a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points, and a closing, and Harrison had decided to talk about his grandfather's hardware store. He pressed start, launched into his hook, and stalled. Two minutes later he had barely finished point one.

"That's impossible," he told Peyton on the phone that night. "Two minutes is too short to say anything important. I need at least ten."

Peyton laughed. "Ten minutes? Nobody would listen past three."

"Then three, minimum." Harrison flopped onto his bed and stared at the ceiling. Something about the two-minute rule bothered him, like a puzzle missing its piece. If two minutes were really too short, why would Mr. Hoang pick it? He grabbed his laptop and typed "famous short speeches" into the search bar.

The answer made him sit straight up. Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, given on November 19, 1863, was about 272 words long and took roughly two minutes to deliver. Harrison read it twice, then counted the words on his own outline: 486. He had been trying to squeeze a ten-minute speech into two minutes. The problem wasn't the time. The problem was everything he refused to cut.

He attacked the outline with a pencil. He would exclude the part about the store's income during the rainy summer, which hurt, because it was his favorite fact. He would cut the list of every tool his grandfather sold. What stayed was the story of the day the whole neighborhood showed up when the store almost closed. That was the hook, that was the heart, and that could land in two minutes.

The next morning he rehearsed for Deborah on the front porch. "Go," she said, and clicked the timer. When he finished his closing line, she held up the phone: one minute fifty-one seconds. Her grin was infectious. "Nine seconds to spare," she said. "Say the Gettysburg thing again, the part about 272 words."

"About 272 words," Harrison said, "and roughly two minutes, November 19, 1863. Same time I just had."

Deborah clicked the timer again. "Once more before the bus comes."

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: In the gold foil experiment, run by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden under Ernest Rutherford, most alpha particles passed straight through, showing an atom is mostly empty space.
story:
Parker stood in the Build-an-Atom workshop at the science museum with a tray of supplies in front of him: blue beads, grey beads, and a fistful of thin copper wire. His best friend Lena slid into the seat beside him and immediately stole three grey beads.

"Those are my neutrons," Parker said.

"They're neutral, they don't care where they live." Lena lined them up on her tray like a tiny jury waiting to judge somebody.

Ms. Ferreira, the workshop leader, walked the rows with her hands behind her back like a museum security guard who could not actually enforce anything. "Today you each build a lithium atom," she announced. "Protons, neutrons, electrons, all in the right places. Go."

Parker got to work. He pushed three blue protons and four grey neutrons into a tight cluster and then, because it looked lonesome, packed more beads around it until his atom was a solid marble of color. He wired on three electrons at the very edge, barely visible.

Lena leaned over. "Yours looks like a meatball. Atoms aren't meatballs."

"You don't know that. Nobody's ever seen one." Parker held it up anyway, and it did look suspiciously like something from a spaghetti dinner.

Last summer, he remembered suddenly, his grandfather had taken him to this same museum. They had stood in the darkened physics hall where a brass contraption sat behind glass, and his grandfather had read the plaque out loud in his big storytelling voice: the gold foil experiment, run by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden under Ernest Rutherford. They had fired alpha particles at a sheet of gold so thin it was barely there. Most of the particles passed straight through, which showed that an atom is mostly empty space. Parker, age ten, had said, "Mostly nothing? Then why does my desk hold my elbows up?" and his grandfather had laughed until a guard glared at them.

"Wait," Parker said now, snapping out of the memory. He pulled the extra beads off his model one by one, dropping them back in the tray with little ticks of sound. Under his fingers the atom went from meatball to a small, lonely cluster with a wire loop swinging far out around it, the electrons rattling like beads on a bracelet three sizes too big.

"Now it looks like nothing," Lena said, but she squinted at her own solid lump, and he could see her deciding he was right. She started unloading hers too, flicking beads at him until he put up his hands like a shield.

Ms. Ferreira stopped at their table and picked up Parker's atom, turning it slowly in the light from the skylight. "Well," she said. "Who told you it was mostly empty space in there?"

"Gold foil," Parker said. "Geiger, Marsden, and the boss, Rutherford."

She raised an eyebrow at Lena's half-dismantled meatball. "And you? Are you biased toward solid atoms, or are you just copying?"

Lena held up her empty tray, beads all dumped, wire loop dangling. "Copying," she admitted. "But from a good source."

Parker spun his atom so the electrons whirred around the quiet middle, and for a second, in the bright museum light, it almost looked like the nothing was something.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Most animals eat more than one kind of food, so real feeding relationships form a food web of many linked chains rather than one single chain.
story:
Elena spread her poster board on the picnic table in the backyard and weighted the corners with rocks from the garden. Mr. Lewandowski had assigned the class a food chain for Monday: sun to plant to animal to top predator, with arrows and labels. Her motivation was simple. She wanted the neatest poster in the class, the one he taped to the wall, and she knew exactly how to get it. Sun, then duckweed, then a snail, then a duck, then a hawk. Clean and straight, like beads on a string.

Maverick dropped his bike on the grass and looked over her shoulder. "Ducks eat duckweed?" he asked.

"All the time," Elena said. She cherished this part of projects, the part where her facts lined up and nobody could argue. "And snails eat the duckweed too. So my chain is sun, duckweed, snail, duck, hawk."

"Wait," Maverick said. "If the duck eats duckweed, and the duck also eats the snail, then your duck is in two places on your poster."

Eena looked at her paper. He was right. She had drawn the duck once, above the snail, but she had also written duckweed next to duck in her notes from the pond book. The duck ate both. She frowned and erased her careful arrow, and the paper smudged. The neat line was gone.

Malachi arrived with a granola bar in his hand and crumbs on his shirt. "That's nutritious, at least," Maverick said, pointing at it. Malachi shrugged and sat down on the table bench. "Whatcha doing?"

"Breaking my project," Elena said. But she was already drawing again. She sketched the duck in the middle of the poster, then drew one arrow from the duckweed to the duck and another from the snail to the duck. Then she thought about the hawk. It probably didn't eat only ducks; it probably took fish too. And the snail, she remembered, wasn't picky either. Every animal on her poster seemed to eat more than one thing.

"It's not one chain," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "It's a bunch of chains stuck together." She drew crossing lines everywhere, sun to plants to snails to ducks to hawk, sun to plants to ducks, fish to hawk. It looked messy and it looked true. She took a new poster board from the garage and started over.

"What are you going to call it?" Malachi asked.

Elena wrote the word across the top in big block letters. "A food web." Then she handed Maverick the green marker. "Draw the duckweed. You're good at plants."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge, and short bursts of it can help a person focus, such as before a test or a race.
story:
The poster on the wall said CALM in big blue letters, which Ariana found funny, because she was the opposite of calm. She sat across from the guidance counsellor's desk, her fingers knotted in her hoodie strings, waiting.

"So," said Mr. Ionescu, "the recital is Friday, and you want to skip it."

"I don't want to skip it," Ariana said. "I want the shaking to stop. My hands shake, my stomach hurts, and last rehearsal I forgot the whole second page of the piece. That's anxiety, right? That's the word my mom uses."

Mr. Ionescu pulled his chair forward. "Tell me what the shaking feels like. Not why it's there. What it does."

Ariana thought that was a strange question, but she tried. "It's like buzzing. Like my whole body woke up." She paused. "Actually, when I forgot the second page, I was in the practice room, comfy, no buzzing at all. And at the last recital, when the buzzing was huge, I played the fast part better than I ever had at home. Weird."

The door opened and Justin stuck his head in. "Mr. Ionescu, the coach says Matis needs to talk to you before his race, he's all jangly." He looked at Ariana. "Oh. Sorry."

"Jangly," Ariana repeated. That was exactly her word for it. Matis got jangly before races, and Matis won races.

"Wait here a second," Mr. Ionescu said, and left. Ariana got up and wandered the office. She found a magnet board with word tiles: stress, coping, boundaries, focus. She slid the tiles around without thinking, and then stopped. Stress. She'd heard that word a hundred times, always bad. But Matis before a race was stressed, and Matis ran his best times. She narrowed her eyes. Maybe the buzzing wasn't a malfunction. Maybe stress was the body answering a challenge, and a short burst of it could actually help a person focus, like before a test or a race. So why had it helped Matis and wrecked her?

She looked at her hands. The difference, she realized, was that Matis never tried to make the jangly feeling evaporate. He jogged in place and let it burn. Ariana fought hers, clenched against it, spent all her energy on the war. She turned the magnet tiles around and spelled out a treaty: she would stop fighting the buzz and let it work.

Mr. Ionescu came back and found her grinning at the board. "Figured something out?"

"I'm going to play Friday," she said. "Shaky hands and all. The shaking is like a spotlight, not a fire alarm."

"Then let's talk coping," he said, sitting down. "What do you do with your hands during a performance?"

Ariana held them out, still faintly buzzing. "Same thing Matis does with his legs before a race," she said. "Nothing. I let them run."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: PolitiFact, a US fact-checking website founded in 2007, rates claims on a scale it calls the Truth-O-Meter, from True to Pants on Fire.
story:
The bus smelled like wet boots and peanut butter, and Romy had been talking about the commercial since the second stop. "It said the candidate made our taxes the highest in the whole country. The whole country. Can you believe that?"

Gabrielle believed approximately none of it, though she said only, "Huh." She had learned from her older brother that the louder a claim got repeated, the more it deserved a slow look. Out the window, a wedge of migratory geese crossed the gray sky, all heading somewhere on schedule, none of them arguing about it.

"The highest in the country," Romy repeated. "My dad yelled at the TV."

"Was it, though?" Gabrielle asked. "Did anybody check?"

Romy shrugged. "It was on TV."

Olivier leaned over the seat, holding his grandmother's pharmacy bag, which he was delivering on the way home and which contained, he announced, a prescription for cough syrup and a box of mints he was absolutely not going to open. "You can't check highest in the country," he said. "That's just somebody's opinion."

"No, it's not," Gabrielle said. "An opinion is like, that candidate has terrible hair. You can't look that up. Taxes you can look up. Somebody keeps the numbers." She thought of the geese again, how they followed rules nobody could see but everybody could test by watching.

Romy crossed her arms. "Fine. Check it, then."

Gabrielle's mother worked evenings and her phone lived in her mother's purse, so Gabrielle borrowed Ms. Liu's phone at the next stop, where Ms. Liu boarded with her umbrella and her crossword. Ms. Liu handed it over with the air of a woman who had already decided sixth graders were beyond surprising. Gabrielle typed the words from the ad, and there it was, a website called PolitiFact, founded in 2007, that rated claims on a scale it called the Truth-O-Meter. She read down the scale out loud. "It goes from True all the way to Pants on Fire."

Olivier laughed so hard he nearly sat on the cough syrup. "Pants on Fire. That's the worst one?"

"That's the worst one," Gabrielle confirmed. She scrolled. The tax claim from the commercial was right there, already checked, and it sat somewhere in the middle, which meant the ad had stretched a small truth into a big one. "So it's not an opinion and it's not a fact," she said. "It's a claim. Claims are the ones you get to test."

Romy peered at the screen, deflating slightly. "So it's not the highest in the country."

"It's not the highest in the country," Gabrielle said. "But try telling your dad that."

Ms. Liu took her phone back, glanced at the page, and said, without looking up from her crossword, "Four letters, 'untruth,' ends in E."

Romy groaned. Olivier wrote LIE on the fogged window with his finger, backwards, so the geese could read it too.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names.
story:
The group chat pinged at 7:40 on a Tuesday night, while Aaron was supposed to be reviewing for his social studies test on the constitution. Adriel had posted a photo of a birthday card, with the message, "My grandfather signed this and it's WRONG and I can't tell if I should fix it before I put it on the shelf." The signature at the bottom read "Kovács Bence." Adriel had captioned it, "He wrote his last name first. He's eighty-three. Is this random or what?"

Aaron zoomed in on the photo. He knew Adriel's grandfather's real name was Bence Kovács, because everyone called him Mr. Kovács, and Adriel called him Bence Papa. So the old man hadn't made a mistake with the letters; he'd made a mistake with the order, or maybe not a mistake at all. Aaron typed, "Was he born in Hungary?" Madilyn answered faster, a thumbs-up and then, "Budapest. Why?" Aaron sat with that for a minute. In class, their teacher had put names on the board in a column, Korean ones like Kim Min-jun and Hungarian ones together, and something about the order had seemed too neat to be a coincidence. He tested it out loud before typing, the way he did with math: if the family name came first in Hungarian, and the same order was used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names, then "Kovács Bence" was exactly right.

He typed it into the chat in two short lines: "In Hungarian the family name goes before the given name. Same order as Chinese, Japanese and Korean names." Madilyn replied, "Wait, so he signed it correctly on purpose?" and Adriel sent, "Hold on, asking him." There was a long silence, long enough that Aaron went back to his notes about the constitution and watched his concentration slowly decompose into checking the chat every twenty seconds.

Then Adriel posted a voice message, thirty seconds long. In it you could hear an old man laughing, warm and unhurried, and saying, "Of course, kisfiam. That is how we write it at home." Adriel typed underneath, "He says thank you for noticing. Also he wants to know if you three are coming for paprikas on Sunday." Madilyn answered immediately, "Yes." Aaron saved the photo of the card, shelf-worthy now, and typed the same.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: During the pubertal growth spurt, hands and feet usually grow first, before the arms, legs and body catch up.
story:
Jade sat on her bedroom floor with three shoeboxes open around her, lacing up the sneakers she had bought in September. Her toes hit the end like a fist against a wall. She unlaced them, pulled them off, and stared at her bare feet, which looked, she thought, like they belonged to somebody else entirely.

"What are you doing?" Yasmina asked from the doorway, holding two mugs of juice she had transported all the way from the kitchen without spilling, an achievement she clearly expected praise for.

"Science," Jade said. "Watch." She lined up her September sneakers, her old sandals from spring, and the sneakers she'd talked her dad into buying two weeks ago, "for backup." The sandals were smallest, the September pair in the middle, and the newest ones fit perfectly. "Three shoe sizes in one year. Three. And look at this." She stood up and pulled at the hem of her jeans. They still reached her ankles fine. Her favorite hoodie still hit her wrists exactly where it always had. "How can my feet be three sizes bigger and the rest of me exactly the same?"

"Maybe you're going to be a yeti," Yasmina said, handing her a mug. "Just feet and then, one terrible day, the rest."

"That's the thing. My brother went through this." Jade flopped onto the bed. "His shoes stopped fitting twice in one school year, and his jeans were fine the whole time. My mom kept saying he was imagining it, and then in the spring he grew four inches in about two months, like the rest of him was just late." She frowned at the ceiling. "So the feet go first. They're like the delivery notice before the package."

Yasmina considered this while drinking her juice. "So your arms and legs and everything are going to catch up?"

"That's my theory. But I want to test it." Jade grabbed the notebook from her nightstand and flipped past the arid, half-finished pages about her vegetable garden, which had died in August and still produced a small stab of resentment every time she saw it. She ruled a fresh chart: date, shoe fit, sleeve length, inseam. "Measurements every Sunday. If my feet are done and nothing else happens for months, I'm wrong. If my sleeves start riding up my wrists next, I'm right."

"Sunday," Yasmina agreed solemnly, as if signing a treaty.

Mr. Desir, their neighbour, knocked then, holding a parcel that had been left at his door by mistake. He glanced at the shoeboxes scattered across the rug and raised an eyebrow. "Cleaning out already? It's not even Christmas."

"Growing," Jade said.

He laughed and set the parcel on her desk. "My mother used to say you can always tell when a kid's about to shoot up. Buy the shoes, wait for the rest."

Jade sat frozen for a second, then looked at Yasmina, who was already grinning. She wrote Sunday's date at the top of the chart and underlined it twice. "First measurement," she said, reaching for the tape measure. "Hold still, wrist."

fact: Lunar New Year, celebrated in China, Korea, Vietnam and elsewhere, falls on a new moon between January 21 and February 20.
story:
Victor had circled February 3 on the calendar in red marker, because that was when Lunar New Year happened, and he had told his whole group that the class project on the celebration would be due right after the community hall dinner. Now he stood in that very hall, holding a plate of dumplings, staring at a banner that read Happy New Year, and feeling the date slide out from under him like a rug.

"You look like your dumpling died," said Noa, who had come with her family from the Korean table across the hall.

"It's January 28," Victor said. "I told Caroline the dinner was in February. The project plan is wrong."

Noa popped a dumpling in her mouth and chewed with vigorous enthusiasm. "My grandma says the date never sits still. It lands on a new moon, somewhere between January 21 and February 20."

"A new moon," Victor repeated. "So the sky decides my grade."

"Take it up with the sky," Noa said, and wandered off toward the rice cakes.

Victor found a quiet corner beside the folding tables and worked it out on a napkin. If the holiday could fall on any new moon inside that window, then it could not coincide with any fixed school date, ever. His plan assumed the celebration would cooperate. It would not. He laughed at himself, which startled an aunt carrying a tray of mandarin oranges, and she gave him one anyway.

He found Caroline by the door, still in her coat. "Good news and bad news," he said. "Bad news, our timeline is garbage. Good news, that's actually the most interesting part. China, Korea, Vietnam, and a bunch of other places all celebrate it, and the date drifts every single year. We can make that the whole project."

Caroline peeled off one glove. "So we turn in a project about a moving target?"

"A moving target we can predict," Victor said, "if we watch the moon."

Behind them, Mr. Chaudhry, who ran the hall, was testing the microphone for the lion dance. "Testing, one, two," his voice boomed. "No revolution on the dance floor, please, only the drummers."

"Sir," Victor called, "did you say revolution?"

"Full turn of the lion," Mr. Chaudhry said, and winked. "Every year it comes around different. Like the holiday, no?"

Victor held up his napkin, covered in numbers, and grinned. "Exactly like the holiday."
